sections.h: Ecclesiastes 5: few words and kept promises
sections.b: Qohelet's advice on vows (Ecclesiastes 5:4–6) closely follows Deuteronomy 23:21–23: when you vow something to God, do not be slow to pay it; not vowing is better than vowing and not paying. He adds two warnings of his own: do not let your mouth bring guilt on you, and do not tell the Temple's messenger that the vow was "unintended" (shegagah, the law's term for an unintentional sin covered by a sacrifice, Leviticus 4:2). The Talmud records Rabbi Meir's view that it is best not to vow at all, against Rabbi Yehuda's that it is best to vow and pay (Nedarim 9a). Christian churches later divided over lifelong religious vows; see the card on Ecclesiastes 5.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 5:1–7; Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Numbers 30:2; Leviticus 4:2; Leviticus 5:4; Matthew 5:33–37

common: Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 is often quoted as a warning against making promises to God lightly.

sections.h: Ecclesiastes 5–6: wealth that does not satisfy
sections.b: Qohelet gives the Bible's most sustained look at the limits of money. The lover of silver never has enough; the more goods, the more mouths to eat them; the worker sleeps while the rich man's fullness keeps him awake (Ecclesiastes 5:10–12). Riches hoarded can vanish in one bad deal, and everyone leaves the world as naked as he came (Ecclesiastes 5:13–17). Some have wealth, honor and many children and are not allowed to enjoy any of it (Ecclesiastes 6:1–6). Yet when God gives a person wealth and the power to enjoy it, that is God's gift (Ecclesiastes 5:19). The New Testament's warnings about the love of money (Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:6–10) stand close to these chapters.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 5:10–20; Ecclesiastes 6:1–9; Job 1:21; Psalm 49:16–17; Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:6–10

sections.h: Ecclesiastes 5:18–20 and 8:15: toil and its share
sections.b: Qohelet calls human work 'amal, toil, and says it brings no lasting gain. But twice in these chapters he commends eating, drinking and seeing good in one's toil as the share God gives (Ecclesiastes 5:18–20; Ecclesiastes 8:15). Joy "will keep him company in his toil". Monastic readers from Jerome on heard the book as a call to contempt of the world; Luther read these verses as praise of ordinary work received with thanks. The "Where Christians differ" card on the book's opening page sets the traditions side by side.

In the middle chapters hevel covers many things: dreams and too many words (Ecclesiastes 5:7), the love of money (Ecclesiastes 5:10), wealth that a stranger eats (Ecclesiastes 6:2), the brief life of a stillborn child (Ecclesiastes 6:4), a fool's laughter (Ecclesiastes 7:6), the wicked praised or forgotten (Ecclesiastes 8:10), and, most sharply, the righteous getting what the wicked deserve (Ecclesiastes 8:14). Life itself is "my days of vapor" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), spent "like a shadow" (Ecclesiastes 6:12), a pairing also found in Psalm 144:4. In 8:14 the word comes close to Michael Fox's "absurd": what happens contradicts what ought to happen.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 5:7; Ecclesiastes 5:10; Ecclesiastes 6:2; Ecclesiastes 6:4; Ecclesiastes 6:12; Ecclesiastes 7:6; Ecclesiastes 7:15; Ecclesiastes 8:10; Ecclesiastes 8:14; Psalm 144:4

sections.b: Qohelet tests the teaching that the righteous prosper and the wicked perish. He has seen a righteous man lost in his righteousness and a wicked man living long (Ecclesiastes 7:15), the wicked buried with honor (Ecclesiastes 8:10), sentence delayed so that people grow bold in evil (Ecclesiastes 8:11), and the righteous getting what fits the deeds of the wicked (Ecclesiastes 8:14). Yet he says he knows it will be good for those who fear God (Ecclesiastes 8:12–13). Scholars read this as a quotation he answers, a later pious gloss, or a tension he will not resolve. The Targum answers with the world to come.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 7:15; Ecclesiastes 8:10–14; Job 21:7; Psalm 73:3–17; Jeremiah 12:1; Malachi 3:15

uncommon: Some scholars think Ecclesiastes 8:12b–13 was added by a later, more traditional editor.

sections.h: Ecclesiastes 8:1–9: advice for the king's servants
sections.b: Qohelet tells courtiers to keep the king's command, mindful of the oath before God; not to storm out of his presence or persist in a cause he dislikes; and to remember that no one can ask him "What are you doing?" (Ecclesiastes 8:2–4). The advice fits officials under Persian or Hellenistic kings. Then Qohelet sets every ruler under limits: no one is master of the wind or of the day of death (Ecclesiastes 8:8). Rashi applied the passage both to God, the King of the world, and to foreign kings, who are to be obeyed in taxes but not in idolatry (Daniel 3:16–18).
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 8:1–9; Ecclesiastes 5:8–9; Proverbs 16:14; Proverbs 24:21; Daniel 3:16–18; Romans 13:1–7

sections.h: Ecclesiastes 7: wisdom's shade and its limits
sections.b: Ecclesiastes 7 holds two thoughts together. Wisdom is good: it shelters like money and gives life to those who have it (Ecclesiastes 7:11–12), and it makes one wise man stronger than ten rulers (Ecclesiastes 7:19). But wisdom cannot be grasped: "I said, 'Let me become wise.' But wisdom stayed far away from me" (Ecclesiastes 7:23), and what has been is "deep, deep down" (Ecclesiastes 7:24). Even the wise man cannot find out the work of God (Ecclesiastes 8:17), as Job 28 also says.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 7:11–12; Ecclesiastes 7:19; Ecclesiastes 7:23–24; Ecclesiastes 8:1; Ecclesiastes 8:17; Job 28:12–28

sections.h: The Persian world of Ecclesiastes 5 and 8
sections.b: Several details of these chapters fit Judea under Persian rule. Judah is a medinah, a province, with officials stacked above officials (Ecclesiastes 5:8), as in Ezra and Nehemiah. The word for a royal "ruling", pitgam (Ecclesiastes 8:11), is a Persian loanword also used in Esther 1:20 and the Aramaic of Ezra and Daniel. Persian kings were remembered for refusing to release sons from military service (Herodotus 4.84; 7.38–39), which gives force to "There is no sending home in battle" (Ecclesiastes 8:8). Some scholars place the book a little later, under the Ptolemies.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 5:8; Ecclesiastes 8:2–4; Ecclesiastes 8:8; Ecclesiastes 8:11; Esther 1:20; Nehemiah 5:4; Nehemiah 5:15

sections.h: Ecclesiastes 7:13–14 and 8:17: what God has bent
sections.b: Qohelet's God governs everything and explains nothing. "Who is able to set straight what he has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13). God made the good day and the bad day to match each other, so that no one can find out what comes after (Ecclesiastes 7:14; compare Isaiah 45:7; Job 2:10). However hard a person toils, even a wise man, no one can find out the work of God (Ecclesiastes 8:17; compare Ecclesiastes 3:11). For Qohelet this is a reason for humility and for enjoying each good day as it comes.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 7:13–14; Ecclesiastes 8:17; Ecclesiastes 3:11; Isaiah 45:7; Job 2:10; Lamentations 3:38; Romans 11:33

sections.b: "God made human beings straight, but they have gone looking for many schemes" (Ecclesiastes 7:29). The verse uses 'adam, humankind, with a plural "they", as in Genesis 1:27. Ecclesiastes Rabbah ties it to Genesis 3: Adam was upright, and "when they became two" they sought schemes. Christian writers such as Augustine used it to teach that God created humans good and that sin came from their own choosing.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 7:29; Ecclesiastes 7:20; Genesis 1:27; Genesis 1:31; Genesis 3:1–7; Romans 5:12

sections.h: Ecclesiastes 7:20: no one who never sins
sections.b: "There is no human being on the earth so righteous that he does good and does not sin" (Ecclesiastes 7:20) agrees with Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:46) and the psalms (Psalm 143:2). Paul's "no one righteous" in Romans 3:10 may echo the Greek of this verse. Churches have read it differently in debates over Christian perfection; see the card on Ecclesiastes 7.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 7:20; 1 Kings 8:46; Psalm 143:2; Proverbs 20:9; Romans 3:10–12; 1 John 1:8

sections.b: The king of Ecclesiastes 1–2 speaks again in 7:23–29. He who had "gained wisdom beyond all" (Ecclesiastes 1:16) confesses that wisdom stayed far away (Ecclesiastes 7:23); the rabbis said he could not understand the law of the red heifer (Ecclesiastes Rabbah on 7:23; Talmud, Yoma 14a). His report of "One man out of a thousand" and no woman (Ecclesiastes 7:28) has long been read against the thousand women of 1 Kings 11:3.

Egyptian harpers' songs, such as the Song from the Tomb of King Intef, say that no one takes his goods with him at death and urge the hearer to enjoy the day, close to Ecclesiastes 5:15–18. Greek writers praised the day of death or said it is best never to be born (Herodotus 1.31; 5.4; Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus), near Ecclesiastes 7:1. These parallels show shared questions across the ancient world. They do not show that Qohelet copied any of these texts, and he differs in naming God as the giver of each day's share.

Two passages in chapter 7 have troubled readers more than any others. "Do not be righteous too much" (Ecclesiastes 7:16) has been read as a golden mean, a warning against self-righteousness (Whybray), God's rebuke to Saul (Talmud, Yoma 22b), and a cynical shrug. The woman "more bitter than death" and "One man out of a thousand" (Ecclesiastes 7:26–28) have been read as misogyny, as a warning about the seductress of Proverbs, as Folly or heresy (Rashi), and as a quoted view that Qohelet tests and rejects with his finding that God made all humankind upright (Ecclesiastes 7:29; Lohfink). The chapter page gives each reading in full.

"Does not everything go to one place?" (Ecclesiastes 6:6) repeats Ecclesiastes 3:20: the long-lived rich man and the stillborn child end in the same grave. No one is master over the day of death, and from that war there is no discharge (Ecclesiastes 8:8). The Targum reads the one place as Gehenna, where sinners go; most modern readers take it as the grave or Sheol, the common lot of all.
